unit_label: Module B unit 6: Operational Risk and Integrated Risk Management

facts.statement: Operational risk arises from deviations from normal and planned functioning of systems, procedures, technology and human failures of omission and commission, showing up as additional expenses or lost opportunities. The Basel Committee defines it as the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events. Its nature: it exists almost everywhere in the organisation; its components vary (some high-frequency low-value, some low-frequency high-severity, the latter more dangerous); and it changes continuously, especially in a changing organisation. Classification by cause: people oriented (negligence, incompetence, insufficient training, integrity, key man), process oriented (transaction based: volume fluctuation, organisational and product complexity; and operational control based: inadequate segregation of duties, supervision, procedures), technology oriented and external causes (disasters, third-party failures). By effect: legal liability, regulatory, compliance and tax penalties, loss or damage to assets, restitution, loss of recourse and write-downs. By event (seven types): internal fraud, external fraud, employment practices and workplace safety, clients, products and business practices, damage to physical assets, business disruption and system failures, and execution, delivery and process management.

The Basel Committee's Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk (June 2011, replacing the 2003 principles) are eleven: (1) the board takes the lead in establishing a strong risk management culture; (2) banks develop, implement and maintain a Framework fully integrated into overall risk management; (3) the board establishes, approves and periodically reviews the Framework and oversees senior management; (4) the board approves and reviews a risk appetite and tolerance statement for operational risk; (5) senior management develops, for the board's approval, a clear, effective and robust governance structure with well defined lines of responsibility; (6) senior management ensures identification and assessment of operational risk in all material products, activities, processes and systems; (7) there is an approval process for all new products, activities, processes and systems that fully assesses operational risk; (8) a process to regularly monitor operational risk profiles and material exposures to losses, with reporting at board, senior management and business line levels; (9) a strong control environment with policies, processes, systems, internal controls and risk mitigation or transfer strategies; (10) business resiliency and continuity plans; (11) public disclosures allow stakeholders to assess the approach to operational risk management. The policy approved by the board should cover the structure, roles and responsibilities, processes and assessment or measurement methodologies.

Organisation for operational risk management: the board takes overall responsibility, approves the framework and a firm-wide definition, and puts in place a comprehensive internal audit system, delegating day-to-day execution; the Operational Risk Management Committee (ORMC) identifies the operational risks, formulates policies and procedures, sets guidelines on assessment and measurement and ensures adequacy of controls, implements the framework throughout the bank and clears new products and processes before introduction; the Operational Risk Management Department (ORMD) is the nodal department for identifying, managing and quantifying operational risk, assesses the risk inherent in all material products, activities, processes and systems, ensures new products are assessed before introduction and monitors risk profiles and reports to senior management and the board; internal audit comprehensively audits the framework, is operationally independent and is not directly responsible for operational risk management. Processes: map key business processes into sub-processes jointly with business groups, take a qualitative approach to aggregating and assessing risks (self-assessment by business groups collated by the ORMD using a scorecard) and use a quantitative approach for new product processes. Monitoring: an incident reporting framework, regular feedback on deterioration of the risk profile, collation of incident data to assess frequency and probability, monitoring of large exposures, and an information system responsive to the framework.

Operational risk is the hardest risk to measure: its behaviour does not follow a normal distribution and loss data take time to accumulate. Basel II options are the Basic Indicator Approach, the Standardised Approach and the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA). Under the Basic Indicator Approach capital is the average over three years of 15 per cent of positive annual gross income (alpha), excluding years of zero or negative income from numerator and denominator; the Reserve Bank's Directions give gross income as net profit plus provisions and contingencies plus operating expenses less excluded items. Under the Standardised Approach activities are divided into eight business lines and the capital charge for each is gross income multiplied by a beta factor: corporate finance 18 per cent, trading and sales 18, retail banking 12, commercial banking 15, payment and settlement 18, agency services 15, asset management 12 and retail brokerage 12; the total is the sum across lines; the courseware notes that 15 per cent alpha is the average of the betas, and that migrating from the Basic Indicator to the Standardised Approach requires the supervisor's approval and documented mapping of activities (the courseware cites application from 1 April 2010 and approval by 30 September 2010). Under the AMA the capital requirement equals the bank's own measurement system output using internal loss data, external loss data, scenario analysis and business environment and internal control factors, subject to supervisory approval; it needs a sound risk management system and is the most expensive. In the Directions, banks in India compute capital under the Basic Indicator Approach.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 462-465, section 16.8; Directions paragraphs 214 to 217

facts.statement: A generic estimate of an operational risk level, as the courseware describes, uses estimated probability of occurrence (scale of 1 negligible to 5 very high), estimated potential financial impact (scale of 5) and estimated impact of internal controls (a fraction of total control valued at 100 per cent): estimated level of operational risk = [probability × impact × (1 − control effectiveness)] raised to the power 0.5. In the courseware's example probability 2, impact 4 and controls 50 per cent give 2.00, called low. Pre-conditions for migrating to the AMA: risk measurement integrated into day-to-day risk management, insurance mitigation restricted to 20 per cent of the exposure, periodic internal or external audit of the measurement process, and loss data (the courseware states a requirement of five years rising to seven years, in a matrix of eight business lines against seven loss event types). The four AMA parameters: internal loss data (the basic building block, collected branch-wise in India), external loss data (scaled to the bank; CORDEx India, a company started in 2010 by 14 Indian banks under the Indian Banks' Association, collects data from banks), scenario analysis (expert opinion with external data to assess high severity events and deviations from correlation assumptions) and business environment and internal control factors (BEICF), incorporated through risk and control self-assessment (RCSA: the unit's assessment of the frequency and severity of potential weaknesses against its existing controls) and key risk indicators (KRIs: variables giving a reliable basis for estimating the loss corresponding to a risk, for example inadequate staffing, many suspense account items, many customer complaints).

Operational risk mitigation lies mainly in the qualitative approach of the framework; insurance may mitigate losses but capital recognition of insurance is available only under the AMA, limited to 20 per cent of the total operational risk capital charge calculated under the AMA, subject to criteria. The courseware says the Basel Committee is contemplating repealing the AMA and replacing it with a Standardised Measurement Approach. The Reserve Bank's Forthcoming Instructions Directions, 2025 provide that the Basic Indicator Approach will be replaced by the Basel III Standardised Approach when the Directions take effect, the effective date to be communicated separately (until then the Capital Adequacy Directions' Basic Indicator Approach applies, and no parallel run is required); the new approach is applicable to commercial banks other than small finance, local area, payments and regional rural banks. Its components: the Business Indicator (BI, a financial-statement based proxy: the sum of the interest, lease and dividend component, the services component and the financial component, each averaged over three years); the Business Indicator Component (BIC = BI times marginal coefficients of 12 per cent up to ₹8,000 crore, 15 per cent above ₹8,000 crore up to ₹2,40,000 crore and 18 per cent above that); and the Internal Loss Multiplier (ILM, a scaling factor based on the bank's average historical losses and the BIC, with the loss component equal to 15 times average annual operational risk losses over 10 years of high quality data, or five years and above if 10 are not available). A bank in bucket 1 (BI up to ₹8,000 crore), or in buckets 2 and 3 without five years of high quality loss data, holds capital equal to the BIC; a bank in buckets 2 or 3 with five or more years holds BIC times ILM. Risk-weighted assets are the capital times 12.5. The courseware (which cites a Master Direction of 15 December 2021 and a loss threshold of ₹1,00,000) says banks not meeting loss data standards must hold at least 100 per cent of the BIC.
facts.locator: Chapter IV paragraphs 22 to 34 and 1(2); Capital Adequacy Directions paragraph 219; S03 printed pp. 466 and 474-475

facts.statement: Integrated risk management is managing all risks generated by all activities across the entire organisation (liquidity, interest rate, market, credit and operational risk). The net effect of all risks is not the sum of the individual risks because of diversification and interplay between risks; integration is a coordinated approach rather than an accounting sum. Comparing firms needs risk-related capital as well as profits, so risk adjusted return on capital (a unit's net income divided by its economic capital) is critical, and a return above the cost of the economic capital adds value (economic value added). Properly implemented it aligns strategic and day-to-day risk, increases transparency for investors and regulators, enhances revenue and earnings and controls downside risk. Challenges: real-time measurement (enterprise-wide data definitions and integrated reporting), business challenges (the real-time environment, global markets, business continuity, technological change, the need to limit earnings volatility) and cultural issues (legacy systems and silos; branches not reporting losses for fear of scrutiny, so loss databases are incomplete). Approach: strategy (risk management as a corporate strategy), organisation (a Chief Risk Officer accountable to the board; the courseware says the Reserve Bank advised in April 2017 that banks appoint a CRO, with a Board-approved policy on the CRO's role, the CRO co-ordinating the risk management department and reporting directly to the MD or CEO), process (common across the enterprise), and systems; top-down policies, integrated limits (for example all outstanding counterparty limits across treasury and credit), integrated reports and integrated systems; the Board through its Risk Management Committee is the apex body.

payload.title: Operational risk and how it is classified
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Basel definition**: **risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events**.

**Nature**: **present almost everywhere**; some risks are **frequent and small**, others **rare and large** (**the rare large ones are more dangerous**); it **keeps changing**, especially when the organisation changes.

| Basis | Categories |
| --- | --- |
| **Cause** | **people** (negligence, incompetence, training, integrity, key man), **process: transaction-based** (volume, complexity) and **control-based** (**segregation of duties, supervision**), **technology**, **external** |
| **Effect** | **legal liability, penalties, loss of assets, restitution, loss of recourse, write-downs** |
| **Event (seven types)** | **internal fraud; external fraud; employment practices and workplace safety; clients, products and business practices; damage to physical assets; business disruption and system failures; execution, delivery and process management** |

payload.title: Measuring operational risk: BIA, standardised and AMA
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Hard to measure**: losses **do not follow a normal distribution** and **data take years**.

**Basic Indicator Approach (the one used in India today)**: **average of 15% × positive annual gross income** over **three years**; **years with zero or negative income are excluded** from numerator and denominator.

**Standardised Approach**: **capital = Σ (gross income of each line × beta)**
| Business line | Beta |
| --- | --- |
| Corporate finance | **18%** |
| Trading and sales | **18%** |
| Payment and settlement | **18%** |
| Commercial banking | **15%** |
| Agency services | **15%** |
| Retail banking | **12%** |
| Asset management | **12%** |
| Retail brokerage | **12%** |

(**15%** alpha = **the average of the betas**.) **Moving up needs supervisor approval** and **documented mapping**.

**AMA**: **capital from the bank's own model** using **internal loss data, external loss data, scenario analysis, business environment and control factors**; **needs supervisory approval**; **the costliest**.

payload.title: AMA inputs: loss data, scenarios, RCSA and KRIs
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Generic estimate of an operational risk level (courseware)**

**Level = [ probability × impact × (1 − control effectiveness) ] ^ 0.5**, with **probability and impact on a 1–5 scale**.

**AMA parameters**
| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal loss data** | the **basic building block**; collected **branch by branch** in India |
| **External loss data** | **scaled to the bank**; **CORDEx India** (**2010**, **14 banks**, **Indian Banks' Association**) pools it |
| **Scenario analysis** | **expert judgment plus external data** for **severe events** and **correlation assumptions** |
| **BEICF** | **business environment and internal control factors**, through **RCSA** and **KRIs** |

**RCSA**: a unit **assesses frequency and severity** of potential weaknesses **against its controls**. **KRI**: a **variable that gives a reliable basis for estimating the loss** from a risk; for example **inadequate staffing, many suspense account items, many customer complaints**.

**Pre-conditions**: measurement **integrated into daily management**, **periodic audit**, **loss history by 8 business lines × 7 event types**, **insurance recognition capped at 20%**.

payload.title: Insurance, the proposed replacement of AMA and the Reserve Bank's new standardised approach
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Mitigation** is mostly **qualitative (framework quality)**. **Insurance** is recognised for capital **only under the AMA**, **up to 20% of the AMA charge**. The courseware says the **Basel Committee plans to scrap AMA** for a **Standardised Measurement Approach**.

**Reserve Bank's Forthcoming Instructions Directions, 2025**: the **Basic Indicator Approach will be replaced by the Basel III Standardised Approach when the Directions take effect**; **the date is to be communicated separately**, so **BIA applies until then** (**no parallel run required**). For commercial banks **other than small finance, local area, payments and regional rural banks**.

| Component | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Business Indicator (BI)** | **financial-statement proxy**: **interest, lease and dividend component + services component + financial component**, each a **three-year average** |
| **BIC** | **BI × marginal coefficients**: **12%** up to **₹8,000 crore**; **15%** to **₹2,40,000 crore**; **18%** above |
| **ILM** | **scaling factor from average losses and BIC**; **loss component = 15 × average annual losses**, from **10 years** of data (**5+ years if 10 are not available**) |

- **Bucket 1** (BI ≤ ₹8,000 crore), or buckets 2 and 3 **without 5 years of good loss data**: **capital = BIC**.
- **Buckets 2 and 3 with 5+ years**: **capital = BIC × ILM**.
- **RWA = capital × 12.5**.

payload.title: Integrated risk management
payload.core_explanation_md:
**IRM** = managing **all risks of all activities together** (**liquidity, interest rate, market, credit, operational**).

- **Total risk is not the sum of the parts**: **diversification and interplay** make the **net effect smaller**; IRM is **coordination**, not adding up.
- **Compare firms on risk-related capital as well as profit**: **RAROC** = **unit net income ÷ economic capital**; a return **above the cost of economic capital adds value** (**economic value added**).
- **Benefits**: **aligns strategy and day-to-day activity**, **transparency for investors and regulators**, **earnings growth**, **controls downside**.

**Challenges**: **real-time measurement** (**common data definitions, integrated reporting**); **business** pressures (**global markets, continuity, technology, earnings volatility**); **culture** (**silos, legacy systems**, branches **not reporting losses** for fear of scrutiny).

**Approach**: **strategy**, **organisation** (**Chief Risk Officer** accountable to the board; courseware: **RBI April 2017** advice that the **CRO reports directly to the MD or CEO**), **common process**, **systems**; **top-down policies**, **integrated limits** (for example **all counterparty limits across treasury and credit**), **integrated reports**; the **Board, through its Risk Management Committee, is the apex body**.
